items.title: For the future of green politics, look beyond the Green party | Zoe Williams
items.summary_raw:
Environmentalists of all political hues must find the language and ideas that turn passion for climate action into impetus

The future of Green politics is under constant discussion after the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, but a much heavier clash – in meaning, symbolism and portent – happened earlier this summer, in King’s Lynn and West Norfolk. The council declared a climate emergency in 2021, along with hundreds of others, and while it was under Conservative control. It is now controlled by independents, and a Reform UK councillor, Austen Moore, moved to scrap the declaration.

It was the end of June, and the meeting had to be called off, because of the extreme heat in the King’s Lynn council chamber. A lot of people paused to grimly remark on that irony, but not Moore, who simply rescheduled the motion for the following week, where it was voted down (by 33 to seven). items.title: Mont Blanc, the ‘roof of Europe’, loses more than a metre of height in a year
items.summary_raw:
Peak of French mountain now 4,807 metres high and fluctuates year by year due to changes in Alpine climate

Western Europe’s highest mountain shrank by more than a metre last year. The peak of Mont Blanc in France now stands 4,807.47 metres above sea level, a team of surveyors said on Wednesday, putting “the roof of Europe” 1.29 metres lower than in 2025.

The mountain is about 4,792 metres tall but the summit constantly shifts as heat, wind and precipitation change the thickness of snow and ice on top. The height scientists recorded during an expedition last month was 1.88 metres greater than it was in 2023, when it reached the lowest levels in recent memory.

items.title: I work for a major insurer. Much of my industry is fudging the numbers in the face of the climate crisis | Anonymous
items.summary_raw:
Insurers are taking on more risk than they should. If – or when – a major disaster hits, the catastrophe will have far-reaching consequences

I work for a major insurer, assessing the risk posed by natural disasters on properties around the world, from family homes to schools, government offices and multibillion-dollar commercial centres. The world is facing greater risk than ever from extreme weather. We are not prepared – and that inaction could have profound consequences for the global financial system.

In the face of ever more extreme and unpredictable climate risks, I am coming under pressure to cut my forecasts for the losses that disasters will cause in order to make insurance more affordable – and get my employer more business. In some instances, the questioning of our numbers and models is justified. But too often, it is not being done to produce more accurate models, but to artificially lower prices. If this is happening at my firm, which is struggling to compete with rivals’ prices, it’s happening elsewhere.

The writer is a modeller working in the insurance industry. A version of this piece originally appeared with the Bureau of Investigative Journali

The standard explanations for why Taiwan is so important to the Chinese Communist Party are familiar: territorial integrity, credibility of deterrence commitments, great power competition with the United States, the strategic value of the first island chain, and the semiconductor industry concentrated in TSMC’s fabrication facilities. These explanations work, but they don’t tell the whole story. items.summary_raw: Two more commercial ships have been targeted by drone strikes just outside Bulgarian territorial waters in the western Black Sea. One of the ships is currently sinking, while the other was damaged.  Shipping data shows that the Turkish-owned "AZOV CONCORD" cargo vessel sunk approximately 17 nautical miles east of Krapets, Bulgaria, while the "CHELSEA 3" cargo ship, which is owned by Ukrainian company "STAR SKY SHIPPING" was damaged approximately 18 nautical miles off the coast of Byala, Bulgaria. "CHELSEA 3" was reportedly hit by three different drones.   The Bulgarian Prime Minister has summoned Russian Ambassador Eleonora Mitrofanova, and is requesting urgent NATO surveillance over the area.

items.title: Trump says Iran wants deal with US but 'don’t know how to'
items.summary_raw:
Trump says Iran wants deal with US but 'don’t know how to'

US President Donald Trump says Iran wants to reach a deal with Washington, but claims "they don’t know how to".

"They want to make a deal, but they don’t know how to,"  he said during a campaign rally in Ohio. 

Trump added that Washington could not allow Tehran to acquire a nuclear weapon, describing the country as "the number one state sponsor of terror".

"Right now, they have no navy, they have no air force, they have no anti-aircraft, they have the worst inflation of any country anywhere in the world, they have no money," the US president said.

items.title: Who are Yemen's Houthis and what do they want?
items.summary_raw:
Who are Yemen's Houthis and what do they want?

Officially known as Ansar Allah, or "helpers of God", the movement emerged in Yemen's far north in the 1990s around the cleric Hussein al-Houthi.

It is rooted in Zaydism, a branch of Shia Islam whose followers are a minority in Yemen but concentrated in the northern highlands.

The group fought six rounds of war with the government of former president Ali Abdullah Saleh between 2004 and 2010. Hussein al-Houthi was killed in the first and leadership passed to his brother, Abdul-Malik al-Houthi, who still heads the movement.

Middle East Eye takes a deeper look:

items.title: Morning update
items.summary_raw:
Morning update

Good morning Middle East Eye readers,

Here are the latest developments: 

  • During a phone call between Iranian foreign minister Abbas Araghchi and his Saudi counterpart Faisal bin Farhan, Araghchi insisted that a military approach in Yemen will complicate the situation in the region. According to Iranian state media, Araghchi had also indicated Iran's readiness in helping start dialogue between Saudi Arabia and Yemen. 

  • Air strikes were reported on the Hamdan district in Sanaa and two more strikes on al-Zurbi Road in the Hayfan district in Taiz, according to Yemen’s Houthi-run Saba news agency. Missile attacks were also later reported on the border district of al-Dhaher in Saada province.

  • A drone attack on a vessel off the coast of Oman left two Indian nations missing

Iran’s security chief claimed on Sunday that US President Donald Trump's adminitation hired “thugs” in the coastal waters of Oman to smuggle oil through the Iranian blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.

Trump “claims every day that the Strait of Hormuz is open, but in response I say: ‘You are smuggling, but the strait is under Iranian control and we manage it,'” Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei was quoted as saying by Iran's ISNA news agency.

Rezaei said that the smuggling operation involves the UAE military and the commander of US Central Command (Centcom), using a handful of “small vessels to transfer oil to larger tankers” and that Iran targets them “every night”.

Russia’s GRU military intelligence agency is reportedly working more closely with organized crime groups and cross-border networks to plan attacks and monitor potential targets.  Several defense companies have increased security for their executives, while others have relocated production sites over Russian threats.  Source: FT

And on Friday night, he'll rally with President Donald Trump in Syracuse. It is not exactly a message that seems geared toward winning over moderate voters. At a political moment where Republicans are hoping to capture centrists wary of an ascendent progressive left, Blakeman has instead embraced the president and his aggressive conservative tactics. The approach has puzzled some in a state where Democrats outnumber Republicans by more than 2-to-1.

The climate crisis is already causing floods, wildfires, drought and record heat. AI agents are already escaping super-secure environments to hack into systems they’re supposed to avoid.

Robert Reich, a former US secretary of labor, is a professor of public policy emeritus at the University of California, Berkeley. items.title: Isaias strengthens to become first Atlantic hurricane of 2026 season
items.summary_raw:
Storm expected to make landfall on US’s northern Gulf coast with risk of flash floods and isolated river flooding

Isaias has become the first Atlantic hurricane of the 2026 season, with wind speeds of 80mph and a minimum pressure of 975mb. It is expected to strengthen to a category 2 hurricane as it approaches the US’s northern Gulf coast on Friday, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).

As a result of the strong El Niño, it has been a notably quiet Atlantic hurricane season. The first hurricane of the season has not formed this late since 8 October 1905, which pre-dates the satellite era (1960s) for tracking hurricanes that has allowed for more non-landfall hurricanes to be discovered.

The apparent error appears in a chapter on net zero in The Right Way, a 100-page policy document produced for the Conservative conference in Birmingham. Badenoch repeatedly used the phrase in her main speech.

items.summary_raw:
Exclusive: Firms made more than £340m last year from processing industrial and commercial wastewater at sewage works that are unable to remove many chemical pollutants

Water companies in the UK made more than £340m in revenue last year by pouring billions of litres of industrial and commercial wastewater into sewage treatment works that experts say are not designed to remove most chemicals, leaving pollutants to pass into rivers, seas and farmland.

Water companies are required by law to take industrial wastewater and issue permits called “trade-effluent consents” that allow businesses to send it to sewage works, though water companies can refuse applications.

items.title: MoD has objected to four windfarms in past year over radar interference fears
items.summary_raw:
Complaints risks putting defence ministry on collision course with Department for Energy Security and Net Zero

The Ministry of Defence has objected to at least four planned windfarms in the past year over fears the spinning blades could cause “unacceptable interference” with radars used to detect military aircraft.

MoD officials raised concerns in late June over plans for an onshore windfarm in County Durham that could result in aircraft “not being detected” within an RAF Low Flying Area, according to a letter to Britain’s planning authority.

items.summary_raw:
Iran will not abandon uranium enrichment, nuclear chief says

Iran will not abandon uranium enrichment or hand over its uranium, the head of the country's Atomic Energy Organisation, Mohammad Eslami, said on Thursday.

Eslami said new US threats against Iran's nuclear sites were "nothing new" and that enrichment was "an inseparable part" of the nuclear process, state media reported.

items.summary_raw:
Turkey assesses defensive support for Saudi Arabia amid Houthi attacks

Turkey is assessing how it can help Saudi Arabia defend against attacks by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi movement under a joint defence pact with Pakistan, Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said on Thursday, ruling out Turkish participation in offensive operations.

Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement in August, under which an armed attack on one member is considered an attack on all. The three countries have since held political and military meetings following Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, with the countries agreeing on Monday to immediately implement their collective defence commitments and ensure the rapid deployment of military forces and capabilities in Saudi Arabia.

"He's working on the Iran deal and doing very well. I think the deal isn't really something that I want to do, but they're willing to offer us anything to stop," Trump said during a campaign rally in Texas.

"They will never have a nuclear weapon," he added.

The US president also expressed that he expects the war on Iran to end soon, saying: "That war ends - it's going to be very soon. It's got to be very soon," he said, describing Iran as "a failed nation."

items.title: This is one of Norway’s most pristine fjords. So why is it being used as a dumping site for mine waste?
items.summary_raw:
The Norwegian government has given a permit to a mining company to release waste into Førde fjord despite a 17-year battle by campaigners and a supreme court ruling against it

Shortly after the Norwegian stock market closed on 17 June 2026, a few dozen local people from the small west coast town of Vevring crowded around a laptop in a school. Surrounded by children’s drawings and windows looking out over Førde fjord, they listened as news arrived from Oslo. Norway’s supreme court had ruled against its government: a permit to release mining waste directly into the fjord two miles upstream was illegal, the court said.

The moment marked the end of a 17-year fight, one of Norway’s most protracted environmental battles in living memory. In Oslo, Ingvild Fonn Asmervik, the project leader for Naturvernforbundet (Friends of the Earth Norway), compared the joy she felt to giving birth to her child. For Anne-Line Thingnes Førsund, a third-generation fisher living on the banks of the fjord in Vevring and a volunteer for the charity’s local branch, it was more of a relief. Like a mountain lifting off her shoulders, she said.

items.title: World must change way it produces food to avoid biodiversity collapse, says WWF
items.summary_raw:
Recovery of tigers, tuna and green sea turtles show nature loss can be reversed when action taken, charity says

Conservation comebacks for wild tigers, tuna and green​ sea turtles prove that global nature loss can be reversed, ​scientists have said. ​But a report warns food production must be the next ​“positive tipping point​” if the world is to avert biodiversity collapse.

The World Wildlife Fund (WWF) analysed nearly 36,000 animal populations and more than 5,000 species, producing the largest ever database of vertebrate wildlife. Scientists found populations had declined by an average of 73% since 1970, showing that “nature continues to be degraded at an alarming scale”, with “no sign of losses slowing”.

items.title: U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle reportedly pressured Trump donor Eric Deters to pay her $100,000 American Express bill shortly before her July 2025 Senate confirmation…
items.summary_raw: U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle reportedly pressured Trump donor Eric Deters to pay her $100,000 American Express bill shortly before her July 2025 Senate confirmation hearing, suggesting he wire the money directly to avoid leaving a paper trail.  Guilfoyle, Donald Trump Jr.’s former fiancée, allegedly offered to use her connections to help Deters with IRS and Justice Department matters and secure a Tucker Carlson interview, for which he had promised up to $1 million.  Messages show Guilfoyle repeatedly warned Deters against documenting their financial arrangements, saying he could cost her the ambassadorship.  Deters, who had previously paid Guilfoyle $300,000 in speaking fees, refused to pay the credit card bill and said she had delivered none of the favors he sought.  Guilfoyle’s lawyer disputed the authenticity of the messages and maintained that she was owed money for previous speaking engagements.  Source: WSJ
